title: the Samkhya Karika)
hook: a spoonful of yesterday's curd in warm milk, and the yogurt that was already there

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika reasoned its way to the witness: a bed is made for a sleeper outside it. What arrangement did you notice was made for someone? A new week begins. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.
screen: `A BED FOR SOMEONE.` · `THE EFFECT IN THE CAUSE.`

segments.voice: Late at night in a kitchen, someone warms a pot of milk, lets it cool until it's just warm to the finger, and stirs in a spoonful of yesterday's curd. A lid goes on. The pot goes somewhere quiet. By morning, it's yogurt. Nobody added yogurt to it. Nobody built it. And the same trick does nothing to a pot of water. So where was the yogurt last night? Samkhya has a bold answer to that question, and it uses the answer to explain the whole universe. Today the Samkhya Karika argues about cause and effect.
screen: `MILK, A SPOON OF CURD, A NIGHT.` → `NOBODY BUILT THE YOGURT.` → `WHERE WAS IT LAST NIGHT?`

segments.voice: Samkhya's answer: the yogurt was already in the milk. Not visible, not yet set, but there. The effect exists in its cause before it shows itself. The Karika gives its reasons in one tight verse, and the verse ends with the claim itself, sat karyam: the effect already is. That's why the view is called satkarya. What doesn't exist at all can't be produced. You need the right material to start with. Not everything comes from everything. A cause can only produce what it's capable of. And the effect has the same nature as its cause. Commentators reach for examples like these: press sesame seeds and you get oil, press sand all day and you get none. The oil was in the sesame. Now watch what this does for the days ahead. If effects are already hidden in causes, then the whole world was already folded inside prakriti, the root. Creation, for Samkhya, isn't making something out of nothing. It's unfolding, the way the yogurt unfolds from the milk, and Samkhya teachers add that the world can fold back in again. Not every school agrees. Nyaya and Vaisheshika, whom we met just before Samkhya, argue that a pot is a genuinely new thing that didn't exist before the potter made it. The two sides argued it out at length, and Hindu tradition keeps both arguments in the room. Samkhya's view also changes how a beginning looks. A seed, a child, a first draft. Whatever comes out of them, Samkhya would say, is already in there, waiting for its conditions.
screen: `THE EFFECT IS ALREADY IN THE CAUSE.` · `ONE VERSE, A STRING OF REASONS.` · `CREATION AS UNFOLDING.` · `NYAYA SAYS: THE POT IS NEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with what's folded in. Settle, and let your breath slow. Each in-breath already holds the out-breath that will follow it. Feel that for a few rounds. Then bring to mind one beginning in your life right now: a project, a friendship, a habit, a child. Don't push it. Just look at it the way Samkhya looks at milk, as something already holding what it will become, needing only time and warmth. If you pray, you can hold that beginning in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Samkhya Karika. Its argument on causes: the effect already exists in its cause, so the world unfolds from prakriti instead of appearing from nothing.
Your line: the Samkhya Karika. Today, find one small beginning, a seed, a sketch, a first sentence, and ask what's already folded inside it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy learn the debate over causation, Samkhya's view that the effect pre-exists in its cause against the Nyaya-Vaisheshika view that it is newly made, as a long-running argument between the schools.
